correctness.rationale: For every \(n\ge1\) and integers \(r\ge2\), \(\lfloor r/2\rfloor<q\le r\), disjoint supporter sets for two outgoing or incoming arcs would have total size at least \(2q>r\), contradicting path functionality. Thus the union containing one spanning path can only be that path or its cyclic closure. Every constituent path of the cycle removes one arc; its removal multiplicity at most \(r-q\) is exactly the quorum condition. This yields a bijection with capped allocations of r named omissions into n cycle arcs, with unique cyclic scaffold and no double counting, plus \(n!\) repeated-order cases. Positive allocations establish precisely the claimed allowed diversity s and smallest n; explicit 3-vertex constructions prove the threshold sharp. The packaged checker exhaustively verified eight parameter triples, including \(n=5,r=3,q=2\) and \(n=4,r=4,q=3\); these tests supplement rather than replace the proof. \(n=1\), \(q=r\), and small n are included.

value.rationale: The object arises naturally when multiple successor predicates are available in two-variable finite-model logic: a first-order sentence can demand quorum support for each actual adjacency. The exact classification reduces apparently independent paths to one cyclic scaffold; this yields complete labelled counts, every possible number of distinct orders, a sharp onset \(n\ge\lceil r/(r-q)\rceil\), and the surprising exclusion of diversity exactly two. A threshold counterexample establishes that strict majority, rather than arbitrary positive support, is structurally decisive. The result is not claimed as a new general decision algorithm and relies on no arbitrary fixed finite cutoff.
